lesson.title: Service Mesh: Traffic Cops for Microservices
lesson.summary: A service mesh manages service to service traffic in a microservices architecture by routing every call through a small proxy alongside each service, applying retries, encryption, and observability centrally rather than in application code.
lesson.body:
NFV showed that a network function like a firewall or load balancer does not need to live in a dedicated hardware box, it can run as software instead. A service mesh takes a similar idea and applies it at a much finer grain: instead of one virtualized function serving an entire site or data center, a small proxy runs alongside every single instance of every microservice, handling the network concerns for that one service instance specifically.

This problem shows up once an application is broken into microservices that talk to each other over the application layer, typically HTTP or gRPC calls between services rather than function calls within one program. A system with a handful of services can get away with each team hand writing its own retry logic, timeouts, and encryption. A system with dozens or hundreds of independently deployed services cannot: that logic gets duplicated inconsistently across teams, written in different languages, and is hard to observe or change centrally. A service mesh addresses this by deploying a lightweight proxy, commonly called a sidecar, next to each service instance, and routing all of that service's inbound and outbound traffic through its own sidecar. The sidecars are then managed centrally by a control plane that pushes configuration, routing rules, security policy, retry and timeout settings, to every proxy in the mesh.

Istio, built around the Envoy proxy, is a well known real example of this pattern. Every service instance gets an Envoy sidecar, and Istio's control plane configures those sidecars uniformly. With that in place, an operator can require mutual TLS encryption between every service in the mesh without any individual service's code knowing encryption is happening, since the sidecar handles it transparently. They can also do things like canary releases: send 5 percent of traffic bound for the payments service to a new version while the rest keeps going to the stable version, watch error rates, and shift more traffic over gradually, all configured centrally rather than built into the payments service itself.

Picture an online store with separate services for the shopping cart, the product catalog, and payment processing, each deployed and scaled independently. Without a service mesh, if the payments service is slow or briefly unavailable, the cart service needs its own retry and timeout logic to avoid cascading failures, and someone needs to build dashboards to see how often that is happening. With a service mesh, the sidecars handle retries and timeouts uniformly, mutual TLS keeps traffic between services encrypted even inside a supposedly trusted internal network, and the mesh's telemetry gives a consistent view of latency and error rates across every service, all without the cart or payments teams writing any of that networking logic themselves.
